sentences.text: Of course, competition will remain a permanent feature of international relations.
But competition does not have to mean confrontation.
Healthy competition can drive innovation, strengthen resilience, and expand opportunity.
But only when it operates within the frameworks that preserve stability and enable cooperation where cooperation is indispensable.

Military power alone cannot secure peace.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary General, First Lady of the United States, distinguished delegates, ambassadors, and fellow leaders, it's my great honor to welcome the world to America as we celebrate 250 years of glorious freedom and independence.
Two and a half centuries after the cause of liberty found its home, on this continent, I can report to you with pride that America is back and our country is stronger today than ever before.
Our economy is the envy of the world.
Our military is the most powerful on Earth.
Our technology is second to none, and we are leading in virtually everything.
Our energy is fueling the planet.
America is rising.
Our nation is growing.
Our power is expanding.
Our country is doing better than ever before.
And our future is very, very bright.
Since I took office, we have created more than 1 million new private sector jobs, and more Americans are working today by far than ever before.
Last week, it was announced that the poverty rate has reached its lowest level in American history.
We lifted 1.5 million Americans out of poverty last year alone, another record.
The African American and Hispanic American poverty rates are at all-time lows.
Real household incomes for Americans have soared to the highest level in history, $87,000 on average, surpassing the prior record that I set in my first term.
From day one, my administration has worked to remove every single unnecessary regulation and obstacle to doing business in America.
We passed the largest tax cuts in American history, and as a result, more money is being invested in the United States right now than has ever been invested in any nation anywhere in the world.

U.S. stock markets have set 80 all-time records, and that's just in the last 12 months, we've secured commitments for $21 trillion in new investments from all over the planet, compared to less than $1 trillion in four years in the previous administration.
Two years ago, our country was dead.
And now we have the hottest country anywhere in the world.
Before I took office, we had the worst and most dangerous border on Earth.
And now we have the most secure border in American history.
Nobody comes in unless they're invited, unless they have permission.
In the past 16 months, zero illegal aliens have been admitted to the United States.
And that's done by some very sophisticated people.
It's not done by the Trump administration.
Zero.
As a result, last year, we achieved the largest drop in violent crime ever recorded.
The murder rate has plummeted to its lowest level in 125 years since the year 1900.
I sent our crime Busters into Memphis, TN and New Orleans, LA, and crime in each place went down over 80% and it'll go down still further.
More importantly, when I arrived on January 20th of last year in Washington, DC, it was riddled with crime.
And now crime is down 87%.
And we're going for 100.
Tourism is -- if you take a look, and I guess a lot of you have been there, tourism is thriving.
Restaurants are bustling.
And people are proud of our nation's capital.
They're proud like never before.
We've invested more money in the United States military in the past 12 months than ever before.
And this term, it'll be $1.5 trillion.
We inherited a dark age of America from the previous administration, and we turned it into the golden age of America.
The entire world is being lifted by the wealth, strength, spirit, and momentum of a newly energized and a very powerful United States of America.
And just as we moved quickly to address problems we inherited at home, We have acted with decisiveness and speed to reshape the world stage and solve problems that have plagued us for far too long.
Every leader in this room and your great leaders, many great leaders, I know all of you very well.
But they know that given only a short time to make this world better, safer, and more prosperous for our children, for the people on Earth, we have to take advantage of it.
As president of the most extraordinary nation in history, I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day.
I do not believe in letting problems fester.
They only become harder to solve.
So while others have talked, I have acted.
While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace.
While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them.
While others have talked of courage, America has shown it.
While others have promised strength, I have used it to make America the most powerful country in the world.
Working with many nations in this room, we are solving decades of intractable challenges, and we are settling years of unfinished business.

divides and problems which erode citizens trust in democratic institutions and authorities.

The first major challenge we face is the frontal assault we must wage on organized crime and petty crime.
Peru is located on a continent in which there are no wars between nations.
However, we are faced with another type of war, that is that declared by transnational criminal organizations, organizations that have sowed terror among our people.
In this war, There are no battle grounds, no fronts.
Indeed, no fronts have been defined.
There are no international rules governing these conflicts.

sentences.text: Thank you very much.
On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President of the Republic of Finland.
The Assembly will hear an address by His Royal Highness Grand Duke Guillaume of Luxembourg.
I request protocol to escort His Royal Highness and invite him to address the Assembly.
Madam President, Excellencies, first and foremost, allow me to extend my warmest congratulations to His Excellency Dr. Kalliloh Raman on his election as President of the General Assembly.
He can certainly count on Luxembourg's full support throughout his tenure.
Madam President, the theme that has been chosen for this General Debate can hardly be more timely.
When I try to paint an honest picture of the world we live in, one thing strikes me in particular.
Trust is under growing strain.
Trust between nations, trust between people, and perhaps most importantly, trust in our ability to work together.
And yet, I believe that trust is precisely where we should begin.
Not because trust is easy, but because every lasting achievement of the international community has begun with a decision to trust.
This is my first address to this Assembly as Head of State of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg.

I assumed office less than a year ago, It is therefore a particular honor to stand before you today and to reaffirm from this podium the importance Luxembourg attaches to the United Nations and to a rule-based international order grounded in the rule of law.

sentences.text: But this moment also makes me reflect on what the United Nations means from the perspective of my own generation.
As a relatively young man who has had the privilege of traveling the world, I have been fortunate to meet people from very different cultures, backgrounds, and traditions.
These experiences have left me with a simple and lasting conviction.
We can learn a lot from each other.
And I remain convinced that it is only by working together that we can overcome the many challenges our world is facing today.
This conviction is not naive.
I am fully aware of the difficulties confronting us.
But precisely because the world is becoming more difficult, I believe we must resist the temptation to give up on cooperation.
There has never been a time when communication between people in different parts of the world was so easy.
Millions of young people have virtual friends and acquaintances across continents through social media, gaming, and countless other forms of connection.
We have never been so connected, and yet we seem increasingly unable to trust one another.
This should make us reflect.
Is it still possible to build a world order in which respect and the willingness to work towards common goals can prevail over the pursuit of self-interest and power?

sentences.text: I have traveled far to speak on matters that may seem distinct, but are united by a single fundamental principle: the right of every people to be treated as an equal and to speak for itself.
Mr. President, there are moments in the life of a nation when its people are called to remember who they have always been.
This is such a moment for us.
And so I begin with something deeply personal to my people and my country, and that is our name.
For many years, the world has known our country as Nauru.
Nauru is how our name sounded to those who found it hard to say, and the world kept it.
but it is not the name our people used among themselves.
I rise on my first point not to announce a change, but to affirm a truth.
Long before our country took its place among the family of nations, long before our name appeared on international records, our people knew our homeland by one name, Nauru.
That name carries the memory of our ancestors, our language and our identity.
It has been there all along, never lost, never absent.
Today we restore Nauru.
We did not make this choice to erase our past.
We make it because we honour it.
We do so with respect for our history and with gratitude for the journey Nauru has carried us through to our independence and our place on the international stage.
Mr. President, My government's priority is investing in our people and our future generations.
Restoring our name gives back to them a piece of the inheritance because the identity handed down by our own ancestors has a place in the community of nations.

Mr. President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, I stand before you today not as a Prime Minister, but as a salesman.
And I am here not to sell you a product, or a policy, or yet another declaration.
I am here to sell you An idea.
An idea conceived and spearheaded by His Majesty King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck.
An idea embraced by the people of Bhutan.
An idea already being built.
That idea is Gyalpo Mindfulness City.
And my sales pitch is simple.
Come and build it with us.
Now, the world has built new cities before.
Financial centers, free ports, technology hubs, special economic zones.
But GMC is different.
You see, Gailipoo Mindfulness City is a special administrative region, an SAR.
Under its royal charter, GMC exercises full autonomy in governance, legislation, and the judiciary.
Think one country, two systems.
Think of the agility of a microstate.
But GMC was not inherited from history.
It was not created to manage a transfer of sovereignty.
It is being deliberately created by Bhutan, within Bhutan, on sovereign Bhutanese territory for the future.
GMC covers more than 4,000 square kilometers.
That is more than five times the size of Singapore.
But its greatest opportunity is not its size.
Its greatest opportunity is an institutional blank slate.
GMC was given something extraordinarily rare, the freedom to design an entire city and its operating systems from first principles.
So we asked, If you could begin again, how would you govern?
What laws would you write?

Our people are educated.
But our economy is small.
It cannot yet create enough opportunities for our young people.
So too many of them leave home to find opportunity elsewhere.
For a country as small as ours, this is not only an economic challenge, it is an existential one.
We cannot simply tell them to stay.
We must give them a reason to stay and a reason to return.
Jobs, opportunities, enterprise, a future.
So Bhutan must transform.
But we refuse to believe that transformation requires us to become somebody else.
We want economic growth.
We want investment.
We want technology.
We want successful companies.
We want our people to become wealthier.
But we also want to protect what makes Bhutan, Bhutan.
That is the driving force behind His Majesty's vision for GMC.
And that is why His Majesty is personally spearheading its development.
GMC is not a project on the margins of Bhutan.
It is at the heart of our national transformation.
Our people have embraced GMC as a people's project, an investment in our children, our economy, and our shared future.
Bhutan is not waiting to see whether the world believes in GMC before committing to it.
We have committed, fully.
Now let me tell you why GMC is built to succeed.
Begin with location.
GMC sits directly on the border with India, our closest friend and neighbor.
The vision enjoys the support of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the government of India, and our neighbors across the border in Assam.
Beyond that border lies the world's most populous country and one of its largest and fastest growing economies.
GMC is also a gateway to the markets of South Asia and Southeast Asia.
So GMC begins with what many new cities spent decades trying to acquire.
Access to vast and growing markets, connectivity, and in India, a trusted friend.
Bhutan brings another advantage, one that cannot be bought.
Trust.
Trust built through peace, political stability, the rule of law, and a record for honoring our commitments.
For long-term investors, trust creates something invaluable.
Predictability.
Bhutan has spent generations building that trust.
GMC puts it to work.
Then there is nature.
Imagine GMC in the morning.
Mist rising from its rivers.
forest stretching towards the mountains, elephants moving through the landscape, tigers still roaming its forest.
This is not empty land.
It is a living, carbon-negative landscape, a biodiversity hotspot.

GMC is not asking investors to choose between commercial success and quality of life.
It is designed for both.

They choose where to build their lives.

The Royal Charter is in force.
Laws have been enacted.

The journey has begun.
But there is still an extraordinary opportunity to help define where it goes.
And perhaps the best way to understand GMC is to imagine it as a startup.
a 4,000 square kilometre start-up.
Now, most start-ups begin with an idea, then search for the conditions they need to succeed.

GMC begins with many of them already in place: His Majesty's leadership, an entire country fully committed, land and clean energy, full autonomy, trusted laws and institutions, access to vast and growing markets.
So GMC is a startup designed from the beginning for success.
And there is one guarantee I can give you.
Bhutan will not hedge its bets.
We are all in.
But every startup needs one more critical ingredient, co-founders.
And that, Excellency, is why this salesman is standing before you.
We want your capital, your technology, your talent, your ideas, your enterprise.
And let me be absolutely clear.
We want you to make money.
GMC is not a retreat from capitalism, technology, or ambition.
It is designed to harness all three without sacrificing nature, culture, or human well-being.
Those who come early can help create the industries and markets that others will later enter.
They can help define GMC's economic journey and share in the value they create.
That is a first mover advantage.
At GMC, Commercial success and human flourishing are designed to build on one another.
This balance is deeply Bhutanese.
For more than half a century, Bhutan has pursued gross national happiness.
It does not reject economic growth, but it does ask the essential question, what is growth for?
GMC gives this development philosophy contemporary form through markets, technology, and investment.
But that aspiration itself is older.

For centuries, the Himalayan Buddhist world has carried an ideal of an enlightened society, where material prosperity and spiritual wisdom coexist, where good governance serves human flourishing, and where people live in harmony with one another and with nature.
That ideal is called Shambhala.
Some of our spiritual masters have looked at what is taking shape in GMC and have said, "Under an enlightened king, Shambhala is being built."
Now we make no claim to perfection.
For us, Shambhala points not back to the past, but forward, a promise to carry its wisdom to the future, to build a city that prospers and has a soul.
Mr. President, I told you at the beginning that I come here as a salesman.
Now you know what I am selling.
Kefu Mindfulness City.

Come to GMC.
Help define the journey.
Build it with us.
Become our co-founders.

The future is built.

sentences.text: Thank you so very much.
On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Prime Minister of Japan.
The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Andy Burnham, Prime Minister and First Lord of the Treasury of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.
Madam President, Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen.
As the new British Prime Minister, I'm here today to tell you how Britain will deliver leadership in a changing world for the decade that lies ahead, learning from our experience of the last one.
It is now 10 years since Brexit.
My country has lived through the disruption it brought, and it has given us a unique perspective that I want to share with you today.
Britain is back.
We are restoring our stability, building a more dynamic economy, a nation that wants to trade with the world and work together to solve the shared problems we face.
But we have also learned that we need to adapt to meet the challenge of these times.
We need to rebalance power in our country and bring it closer to people.
We need to work harder to fight the forces of division and instability which threaten us.
Not just through hard power, but through softer, slower means that sow fear and despair.
We need to do more to help people with the everyday cost of living and seize the opportunities that give them hope for the future.
And we need to embrace the incredible potential of technology to improve people's lives.

Overcoming the forces of division and instability starts with national security.
So we will keep investing in our defence, meeting our NATO commitments and strengthening European capabilities.
We will be relentless in building up our hard power and deterrence.
But we will not play Russia's game of trading escalatory rhetoric.
Unlike Russia, we do not seek confrontation.
Instead, we will be prepared but not panicked, clear-eyed but cool-headed.
and unflinching in defending our people and our allies.
True resilience depends on this military strength, but the last 10 years tells us that it is also about something deeper as well.
It is about the strength of the social fabric that binds us together.
There is no national security without a strong, cohesive society underneath it.
That's the starting point for everything we hold dear and everything we want to achieve.
But the fact is, it has been under attack.
In recent years, we have seen industrial-scale assault by hostile actors on the information environment in the UK and that of many of our allies.
Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fears.
They've used bots and fake websites, falsified newspaper articles, forged the branding of 28 British organisations, including universities and the BBC.
They've amplified far-right narratives, And we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 general election.
We also know that they have tried to stoke tensions and unrest in the wake of horrific events.
The idea that anyone would try to use such things to their advantage is just repulsive, but it is what they do.
The Kremlin spends around 1.3 billion pounds each year on manipulating information.

We're talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people's homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community, creating a narrative of decline, stoking division, and sowing despair.
On top of that, we have seen cyber attacks on companies and institutions, and we know that AI will multiply the threat.

to detect, attribute, and disrupt these kinds of hostile state information attacks, to support and defend our democracy.

Maurice Maeterlinck, born in Ghent and awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1911, wrote a strange, almost unsettling play entitled The Blind. 12 people find themselves in a forest on an island.
The guide who led them there is sitting among them.
He is dead, but they don't know it yet.
They are waiting for him to return.
They hear the wind, the sea, the voices around them.
They know they are not alone, yet they can barely tell where the others are.
At one point, one of the characters says, "Years and years we have been together, and we have never seen each other.
That line comes back to me when I look at our world.
We, too, are together.
We meet constantly.
We exchange statements, messages, and positions.
At times, we spend hours around the same tables.
And yet, being in the same room doesn't mean that we understand one another.
Do we still take the time to hear what others are telling us, to understand what they fear, what they need, and what the world looks like from where they stand?
That, to me, is where diplomacy begins.
Not when we agree, but when we no longer do.
Diplomacy is not erasing disagreements, nor about abandoning our principles to secure consensus at any costs.
It is about continuing to speak, continuing to listen, and finding ways to manage our differences without allowing them to lead to a breakdown in relations or to confrontation.
In the play, one of the characters says something very simple.
Let us try to draw a little closer.
Martin Luther King wrote those words more than a century ago.
Yet, they feel entirely relevant today.
Drawing closer doesn't mean thinking alike.
It means refusing to let distance turn into indifference.
then mistrust, until eventually we stop speaking altogether.
That risk is real today.
It is one of the paradoxes of our time.
We have never been more connected, yet we do not necessarily understand one another any better.
Our economies, societies, and technologies has become deeply interdependent, even as the temptation to turn inward returns with force.
In other words, we depend on one another more than ever, at the very moment when we are sometimes tempted to believe that we can do without one another.

The more interdependent we become, the more we need common rules, not to erase our differences, not to impose a single vision of the world, but to ensure that we can manage our disagreements without allowing the law of the strongest to become the only law that matters.
